lead: Mounting makes one file system appear inside another at a directory called the mount point. Sharing lets processes, or hosts, open the same file with defined visibility of changes. The kernel uses a mount table for the first job and open-file entries plus locks for the second. A USB disk, second partition, or network share joins the directory tree this way. Only a few universities teach this chapter.
prereq: You need: path resolution from 5.2; the VFS idea appears in 5.4.

blocks.text: A file system is a set of files and metadata on a device. Mounting attaches it at an existing directory, the mount point, such as /mnt/usb. The kernel records the pair in the mount table. Path resolution (5.2) walks names. At a mount point it consults the mount table and continues at the mounted root. Device /dev/sdb1 may hold a USB file system; /mnt/usb is its visible door. Mount order matters: mount the parent before a child beneath it. At boot the root is first, then /home or a USB disk.
Mounting does not merge directories. The old directory at /mnt/usb is hidden until unmount. After the mount, /mnt/usb/note.txt reaches USB inode 77, not local inode 101.

Unmount removes the mount-table entry and reveals the old directory. It fails if any process has an open file, current directory, or working directory inside; this is a busy mount. Close files and leave the directory first. For nested mounts, unmount the child before the parent. A lazy unmount detaches the name at once and frees the file system when the last user stops. Mounting is privileged because it changes the shared name space.

Each process has a file-descriptor table. A descriptor is a small integer index. It points to an open-file entry holding the current offset, flags, and a pointer to the inode. Two processes can share one open-file entry, or have separate entries for the same inode.

After fork, the child copies descriptors. Parent and child point to the same open-file entry, so they share one offset. An independent open() makes a new entry with a new offset. That is why a read after fork can surprise you.

File locks coordinate shared access. Advisory locks work only if programs check them; mandatory locks are enforced by the kernel. Sharing semantics differ: Unix shows writes immediately; session semantics shows changes after close; immutable-share forbids changes once shared. NFS is a remote Unix-style example; SMB is common on Windows. The VFS in 5.4 gives one interface.

figure.caption: One path, /mnt/usb/note.txt, is resolved through the mount table. After /dev/sdb1 is mounted it returns USB inode 77; before the mount it returned local inode 101, which is now hidden but still open to any process that opened it earlier.

spec.title: Mount lookup
spec.aria: A lookup of /mnt/usb/note.txt goes through the mount table: before mounting /dev/sdb1 it reached hidden local inode 101, and after mounting it reaches USB inode 77.

examples.question: Before any mount, /mnt/usb/note.txt maps to local inode 101. Then /dev/sdb1 is mounted on /mnt/usb, where note.txt maps to USB inode 77. State the inode returned by a read of the same path before and after the mount. What does a process that already opened inode 101 before the mount still read?
steps: Before the mount, path resolution at /mnt/usb uses the local file system, so note.txt gives local inode 101.
The mount table is then changed to map /mnt/usb to /dev/sdb1. The old local directory becomes hidden.
After the mount, the same path resolves inside the USB file system, so note.txt gives USB inode 77.
A process that opened inode 101 before the mount still holds that open-file entry; unmount does not change its inode, though it may see stale data.
examples.answer: A read returns inode 101 before mount and inode 77 after mount; an already-open old file still refers to inode 101.

traps: A mount point hides the old directory; it never merges the two directories.
Unmount can fail with a busy mount; a lazy unmount only detaches the name.
fork shares the open-file offset; a separate open() gives a new offset.
Advisory locks do not stop programs that ignore them.
NFS or SMB caching can delay visibility; do not assume local Unix semantics.

quiz.q: Define mount point and mount table.
quiz.a: A mount point is the directory where a file system is attached. The mount table stores mount point to mounted file system mappings.

quiz.q: Why does the old directory at a mount point vanish?
quiz.a: The mount-table entry redirects lookup to the mounted root. The old directory is hidden, not merged, until unmount.

quiz.q: Using inodes 101 and 77, what does /mnt/usb/note.txt return before and after mounting /dev/sdb1?
Parent and child share a descriptor after fork; parent reads 10 bytes. Why does the child's next read start at offset 10?
quiz.a: Fork copies descriptors to the same open-file entry. Both processes share one offset.
Advisory locks work only if programs check them; mandatory locks are enforced by the kernel.

quiz.q: Can you unmount a file system while a shell's current directory is inside it?
quiz.a: No; the mount is busy. Leave the directory first, or use a lazy unmount.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linux containers use mount namespaces to give each container a private view of the same mount table. Overlay file systems stack a writable layer over read-only images. Search for mount namespaces, overlayfs, NFSv4 delegation, and SMB oplocks.
